segments.text: our hearing room, as well as our online participants.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: I think this is a very important step forward in the quest to make the law accessible to

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: all.

segments.text: Who owns the law?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: I'm glad to be here with my colleague, Dan Lundgren.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: We have often collaborated on law library issues.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: We also both serve on the joint committee with oversight over the Library of Congress,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: and it seems to me that the Library of Congress, really the biggest library in the world, is

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: a good place to start with law.gov.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: Now, having said that the law needs to be accessible.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: And as a bedrock principle, I believe that's true, obviously, there are issues that need

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: to be flushed out and then addressed as we move forward on this effort.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: Someone earlier, as we were talking, waiting for the beginning of this session, said, you

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: know, it's sort of practical privacy.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: When you've got material, Social Security numbers, other matters that are in paper filings,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: they're really not accessible.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: You have to go down to the courthouse.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: You have to get them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: But if they're online, there's a privacy issue that is pretty big, and so we need to deal

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: with that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: privacy and the like.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: So this is a very important session here in Washington.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: I know that Carl is going around the United States to get smart people thinking of what

segments.text: are the barriers?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: How do we overcome them?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: And that's the best way to achieve our goal, which is to make sure that the primary documents

segments.text: having a markup of a bill, and for some reason, the chairman had difficulty distinguishing

segments.text: between Lofgren and Lundgren.

segments.text: people just have their name without a middle name in it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And mine is Daniel E. Lundgren, and I asked why they put it up there, and they said that's

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: to distinguish you from Zoe Lofgren so that there is no error.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So we're very careful around this place.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And also, thank you very much, Carl.

segments.text: About the sixth time you said longstanding, I wondered if I needed to bring a wheelchair

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: or something up here.

segments.text: Both Zoe and I started very, very young, so even though we're longstanding, we are still

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: hopefully vigorous.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I'll try to be brief, which is always strange for people coming from the law profession.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Who's ponderous documents when filed with the courts are known as our briefs, but I

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: will try to be brief.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: In the cacophony of voices in our culture, I don't think there's any doubt that law is

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: so important and often helps us rise above that cacophony.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: You think of the Magna Carta.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: You think of the US Constitution, the Reconstruction Amendments, the Civil Rights Acts, the Geneva

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Conventions, Nuremberg Trials, Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: They form the legal architecture of our culture, of the way in which we go about ordering our

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: lives to some great extent.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: They enshrine some of our most cherished principles.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: They talk about the value of life, the freedom of conscience, religious freedom.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The founders had a phrase.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: In which they said, "The law is king."

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That's sort of an extraordinary sense if you think about it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: It is the idea that we have non-arbitrary law.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We are a country of laws, not of men, in a very real sense.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: You can thank our greatest jurists for their contributions to the law.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Blackstone, the Framers, Justice Marshall, Justice Harlan.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I have to confess, I've not always enjoyed the study of the law, particularly some of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: my semesters in law school.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Perhaps those were the times when I least enjoyed the study of the law.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But even there, and in Congress on the Judiciary Committee when I was privileged to serve as

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Attorney General of my state, and in the one opportunity I had to argue a case before the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: United States Supreme Court, I've come to have a deep and abiding appreciation for our

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: legal history.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: This is important.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I love the title.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The raw materials of our democracy, broader access to primary legal materials in the United

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: States.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Might scare some people if they read that title.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: It basically means allowing people an opportunity to read those documents that are so fundamental.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I am one of those who has for a long period of time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Argue that the Supreme Court is wrong when they don't allow televising of their deliberations.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I can understand why we don't allow it in some circumstances in trials because of undue

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: influence or the undue impact on witnesses and perhaps jurors.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But I find really no relevant argument against televising the deliberations of the Supreme

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Court.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Because in some ways what happens in my judgment is it reminds me of.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That famous movie which ends with the wizard being behind the screen.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And when we make it so difficult to access those who are the final arbiters if you will

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: of issues engaged in the law.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: It creates an artificial mysteriousness that I think is not helpful.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I think we ought to have greater access.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The idea that only people steeped in the law can understand the Constitution because the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: words are so technical.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: What they say is not what they mean to me is an absurdity.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And to the extent that we can grant greater access to the raw materials of our democracy

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: so that people can read them for themselves and attempt to understand them with the meaning

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: of the words found there.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I think the better off we're going to be.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So I for one view this as an interesting argument, interesting subject matter and I will be working

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: along with others.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: To ensure that we do have greater access to these fundamental materials of our democracy.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And in that process I will still work to encourage the Supreme Court to see the wisdom of my ideas.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: It's much easier for me to say that from here than when I was at the podium appearing before the members of the Court.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: that went before me.

segments.text: And about a month before I argued there was a member of the Bar arguing and a question

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: of the members of the Court said.

segments.text: to this or how do you interpret such and such case?"

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And this fellow stopped for a minute and he thought and he finally said, "Well for purposes

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: of the matter before this Court we really don't have to know how that decision was decided."

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: "Council, maybe we don't but you do."

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

body.summary: The discussion revolves around making primary legal materials accessible to all Americans, with concerns about privacy and sensitive information raised as potential obstacles. The concept of 'law.gov' was mentioned as a potential solution to make law accessible online. The Library of Congress makes collective decisions regarding information sharing, preservation, distribution, access, and organization.

The concept of 'law.gov' is mentioned as a potential solution. The Library of Congress plays a key role in decision-making regarding information sharing.
